summary: Points out a possible deadlock in the Initial Connection Protocol. If both sides issue one request and wait for a match before the second, the first requests may not match, and a deadlock can occur when both open send or both open receive sockets.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people both wait for the other to speak first, so nobody talks. The note shows how that can happen when computers say hello.

subtitle: A deadlock hazard when two hosts initialize a connection

tldr.problem: The Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) can deadlock if both hosts issue one request and then wait for a match before sending the second, especially if both attempt to open send sockets or both open receive sockets first.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 202 identifies the race condition and recommends that the server open its send and receive sockets before waiting, and that the user issue multiple requests without waiting for each to match. This overlaps the operations and prevents mutual waiting.
tldr.outcome: The note corrected a hazard in the early ARPANET protocol that could leave two hosts blocked indefinitely.

today: This is a brief errata note correcting a hazard in the Initial Connection Protocol. RFC 202 did not become an independent standard but ensured that implementers of the ICP would understand how to avoid deadlock.

sections.title: The Deadlock
sections.content: The Initial Connection Protocol specifies handshake steps for a server and user to connect. If both sides issue one request for comment (RFC) and wait for it to be acknowledged before issuing a second, deadlock is possible. In particular, if both sides attempt to open their send sockets first, or both attempt to open their receive sockets first, the first RFCs will not match and the connection hangs.
sections.plainLanguage: If both sides do exactly the same thing in the same order, they can get stuck waiting for each other.

sections.title: The Solution
sections.content: RFC 202 recommends two changes: First, the server should perform its open-socket steps before waiting for a user response. Second, the user should issue its RFCs in sequence without waiting for the server to reply to each one. Additionally, if a host must delay between RFCs, it should prioritize issuing the ones on sockets S and U+3 first, as these are critical for breaking the deadlock.
sections.plainLanguage: The server goes first and does not wait; the user sends all its requests quickly. This way neither side gets stuck.

sections.title: Implications
sections.content: This errata clarified a subtle race condition in the ICP that could trap implementations in mutual waiting. By ensuring one side takes initiative and the other side batches its requests, the protocol could proceed reliably. The fix shows that connection setup protocols must carefully order operations to avoid deadlock, a lesson that became central to later transport protocol design.
sections.plainLanguage: Taking turns and not waiting too long keeps things moving. This idea showed up in later connection setup rules.
